title: Progress in the mid-19th century: Nightingale, Chadwick, Snow and Simpson

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Breadth study B2, key topic 1. No class textbook uploaded for this option yet.

learn.intro: In the mid-1800s nobody knew that germs caused disease. Even so, Nightingale improved hospitals, Simpson tackled pain in surgery, Chadwick pushed for public health reform and Snow linked cholera to dirty water.

sections.title: 1. Barriers to progress

blocks.p: The biggest barrier was the lack of understanding of what caused disease. Most doctors believed in miasma — that disease spread through bad air from rotting matter. Some believed in spontaneous generation, the idea that microbes appeared from decaying material. Without knowing about germs, doctors could not prevent infection.

Other barriers: cities were overcrowded with poor housing, little clean water and no proper sewers; governments believed in laissez-faire (not interfering in people's lives); and many doctors resisted new ideas.

evidence: Industrial towns overcrowded with poor sanitation.

sections.title: 2. Florence Nightingale and nursing

blocks.p: During the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale took 38 nurses to the army hospital at Scutari in 1854. She found filthy wards, poor food and overcrowding. She cleaned the hospital, improved hygiene, food and ventilation, and organised the nurses. The death rate among soldiers in the hospital fell dramatically.

Back in Britain she used statistics to argue for reform, wrote Notes on Nursing (1859), and in 1860 opened the Nightingale School of Nursing at St Thomas' Hospital, London. Nursing became a respectable, trained profession for women. She also influenced hospital design, favouring airy 'pavilion' wards — although she believed in miasma rather than germs.

evidence: 1854: Nightingale arrives at Scutari with 38 nurses.

sections.title: 3. Dangers in surgery and Simpson's chloroform

blocks.p: Surgery had three great dangers: pain, infection and bleeding. Without pain relief, surgeons had to operate very quickly; patients could die of shock.

In 1847 James Simpson, an Edinburgh professor, discovered that chloroform was an effective anaesthetic. It became popular after Queen Victoria used it during childbirth in 1853. There was opposition: some patients died from overdoses (Hannah Greener died in 1848), and some people believed pain was natural or God-given.

Anaesthetics solved pain, but surgeons now attempted longer, more complicated operations — so deaths from infection and bleeding could actually rise. This period is sometimes called the 'black period' of surgery.

sections.title: 4. Public health: Chadwick, the 1848 Act, cholera and Snow

blocks.p: Edwin Chadwick's Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population (1842) showed that the poor in towns died much younger than the rich, and argued that cleaning up towns would save money by reducing illness.

Cholera epidemics (1831–32, 1848–49, 1853–54) killed tens of thousands and frightened the government. The Public Health Act (1848) set up a General Board of Health and allowed towns to create local boards of health to improve water and sewers — but it was permissive (not compulsory), so many towns did nothing.

In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths in Soho, London, and showed they clustered around the Broad Street water pump. He had the pump handle removed and cases fell. He proved cholera spread through contaminated water, not miasma — though he could not identify the germ, and many ignored his findings at first.

evidence: 1854: Snow and the Broad Street pump.

vocab.def: The belief that disease spread through bad air.
A law that allows but does not force action.
A disease spreading quickly to many people.

misconceptions.right: She believed in miasma; her hygiene worked even though the theory was wrong.

misconceptions.wrong: Anaesthetics made surgery safe straight away.
misconceptions.right: They removed pain, but infection and bleeding remained — longer operations could increase deaths.

flashcards.q: What was the main barrier to medical progress around 1848?
flashcards.a: No understanding of germs — belief in miasma and spontaneous generation.

flashcards.q: What did Nightingale change at Scutari?
flashcards.a: Cleanliness, ventilation, food, organised nursing — the death rate fell dramatically.

flashcards.q: Why was Nightingale important after the war?
flashcards.a: Notes on Nursing; Nightingale School (1860); trained, respectable nursing; hospital design.

flashcards.q: What were the three problems of surgery?
Why was there opposition to chloroform?
flashcards.a: Overdose deaths (Hannah Greener 1848); belief pain was natural or God-given.

flashcards.q: What did the 1848 Public Health Act do?
flashcards.a: Set up a General Board of Health; allowed towns to improve water and sewers — but was not compulsory.

checklist.text: I can explain the barriers to progress, especially the lack of understanding of the causes of disease.
I can describe Nightingale's changes to nursing and hospitals at Scutari.
I can explain the dangers in surgery and the impact of Simpson and chloroform.
I can explain public health problems, Chadwick, the 1848 Act, cholera and Snow.
